title: The Foundational Importance of Executive Functioning
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article breaks down Executive Functioning, the brain's management system, into four components: working memory, mental flexibility, self-control, and prioritizing, and invites readers to self-assess against each. It explains what strong performance in each area looks like in everyday behavior, from following multi-step directions to resisting distraction and reordering priorities as new information arrives. The piece cites research suggesting these skills largely stabilize after adolescence yet remain a major driver of professional success, framing the topic as foundational to more complex capacities like reasoning, planning, and decision-making.
points: Executive Functioning has four core components: working memory, mental flexibility, self-control, and prioritizing.
Working memory shows up in the ability to retain and apply information while actively using it.
Self-control is defined as suppressing impulses and resisting distraction rather than just staying calm.
Research links these skills strongly to professional success and says they stabilize after adolescence.
quotes: Executive Functioning refers to higher-level cognitive skills that allow people to manage their thoughts, actions, and emotions to achieve goals.

The skills that make up Executive Functioning are often described as the “management system of the brain” because they contribute to planning, organizing, concentration, remembering, and the controlling of impulses.
Instead, they have the self-discipline to regulate their behavior to fit the demands of a situation.
Research confirms that Executive Functions develop throughout childhood and adolescence and then remain relatively stable and unchanging throughout adulthood.
In fact, research confirms that much of the professional success people enjoy in life depends largely upon these four elements in the Executive Functioning skill set.
